Explain.
Mr. GUERIN; Mr. Speaker, this is a very innocuous piece of legislation, but at the same time it is most important so far as our working men are concerned. It is a bill to safeguard their interests. I may say that I have had the experience, the painful experience, lately of noticing that while foreigners were very much in evidence on public works, our own citizens seemed to be idle. I gave several letters to men asking that they be engaged, and to my astonishment very frequently these men-I might call them young men, about 40 to 45 years of age-returned and told me that they had been refused employment because they were past the age limit. There is evidently some form of workmen's insurance taken advantage of by contractors, which, as it places the age limit very low, I suppose they get at a cheap rate. This bill provides that in connection with all government contracts there shall be no age limit so far as working men are concerned, so that our citizens in general may get an opportunity of participating in the benefits of those contracts. The bill also contains a section giving legislative dignity to the fair wage clause that should be incorporated in all contracts.

Mr. Chairman, there is very little difference between the provision of this resolution and those contained in the other two bills which will be considered at a later date. This land in British Columbia was ceded to the federal government for .the purpose of constructing a railway eastward from the Pacific coast to connect with what is now .the Canadian Pacific railway. An area of land twenty miles wide on each side of that line was ceded by the provincial government for this purpose. In addition, as there had been some considerable alienation of land in that territory, three million acres, known as the Peace River block, was added, and for the land ceded for this purpose the governor in council undertook to pay to the government of British Columbia an annual subsidy of $100,000.
Briefly, the act provides that the land shall be re-transferred to the province of Britidi Columbia, and the grant of $100,000 continued. The only difference between this agreement and the agreements with Manitoba and Alberta-and the agreement with Saskatchewan as well, which I hope to introduce in a day or ibwo-is that there are ordnance lands in British Columbia in question, and I believe section 6 of the act deals with those ordnance lands and straightens out some difficulty between the federal and provincial governments as to their administration.

I do not come from British Columbia, but I desire to protest against these provisions. Imagine people living in a vast area the size of Prince Edward Island being governed by regulations made by the governor in council in Ottawa, and then we are told that we are putting the western provinces on an equality with the other provinces of the Dominion. How long does anyone think Ontario or Quebec would tolerate that state of affairs? T et it is to be thrust upon the western provinces; they are to be told that because the Dominion reserves parks in their provinces, a few officials in a departmental office here in Ottawa are to draw up regulations, to be approved by the governor in council, for the government of these areas, and that the legislatures in the respective provinces are to be subordinated to those regulations in respect to taxes, even, if there is a conflict.
That is what it means. The premier of my province informed the legislature, I believe, that he was forced to take this agreement or get nothing. I am not going to anticipate that discussion, but it is a monstrous thing that in the four western provinces, because the Dominion government reserves areas for parks, the people living within those areas shall not have any local home rule at ail; they will be governed by regulations drawn up by a group of officials sitting in Ottawa and approved by the governor in council. If the legislatures of these western provinces pass laws which are in conflict with such regulations. the laws will fall and the regulations prevail. Mr. Chairman, the provisions are the same with respect to all four provinces, and I read from the agreement with Manitoba as follows:
16. The parliament of Canada shall have exclusive legislative jurisdiction within the whole area included within the outer boundaries of each of the said parks, notwithstanding that portions of any such area may not form part of the park proper, and the laws now in force within such areas shall continue so in force only until changed by the parliament of Canada or under its authority, provided, however, that all laws of the province now or hereafter in force, which are not repugnant to any law or regulation made applicable within the said areas or any of them by or under the authority of the parliament of Canada, shall extend to and be enforced within the same, and that all general taxing acts passed by the province shall apply within the same unless expressly excluded from application therein by or under the authority of the .parliament of Canada.
The parliament of Canada can supersede the taxing power of the legislature of the province, and I think most people would regard the creation within the province of an area not subject to the legislature of the province as being something wholly wrong. It denies home rule to the people of that part of the province of British Columbia; that is

what it means. It is no use talking about despotism not being exercised, the fact is that an invitation to despotism usually results in that force being exercised. Permanent officials thrive on despotism. The essay on that subject of the lord chief justice quotes from a number of judgments including the judgment of the court of appeal in England and reference is made to the tendency of officials in that direction.
I should think that the proper way to deal with this matter would be to have the regulations for the administration of the parks which are passed by the governor in council made subject to the approval of the lieutenant governor in council, because the area is part of the province. Perhaps I should not anticipate discussion, but take the Rocky Mountain park and Jasper park in Alberta, and the combined area-I speak subject to correction- is much larger than the area of the province of Nova Scotia. The sum total of the areas of the parks in Alberta is as great as the area of the maritime provinces.

I quite
appreciate the force of the remarks of my hon. friend, but I would like him to realize that the administration of the affairs of the national parks is a big task. At present a minister of the federal government has to endeavour to put into force laws which are only provincial in character. For some considerable time we tried to discover some halfway ground which would be acceptable, but we found that to be a very difficult thing to do. Perhaps the ingenuity of some of my hon. friends will suggest a way out of this difficulty which confronts those of us who are responsible for the administration of the parks. While a park may be within the province of Alberta, all the residents within the boundary of that park must of necessity be under some control by a federal authority, otherwise our task would be a hopeless one. We may have gone too far, but I want to stress the fact that I must have the necessary authority with which to administer those areas which are set aside as national parks. I have no desire to interfere with provincial laws except in so far as they make it difficult to carry on this administration.

I am grateful to the hon. minister for putting his reply in the terms he has. I offered him a sugestion which, were I in his place, I would accept. I agree with him that the federal parks must be administered as such and that the legislative body responsible for maintenance is the parliament of Canada and not the provincial legislatures. However, the people who live within the geographical area of the parks are subject to the operation of the laws not only of the parliament of Canada but of the legislatures of the
provinces. When you have an area within a province which is subject only to federal legislation, you create a situation whereby powers are exercised entirely at variance with those exercised just beyond an arbitrary line. As the law now is, power is granted to the governor in council to enact regulations, and my suggestion is that such regulations should be subject to the approval of the lieutenant-governor in council so that the provincial authorities would not find themselves in a hopeless position with regard to the administration of a part of their territory.

Take the one matter of the preservation of law and order. The authorities of British Columbia are responsible for the preservation of law and order within the territory called British Columbia. The contention of the crown is that the province and not the Dominion is responsible for the maintenance of the troops to preserve order in Nova Scotia. Conceive the possibility of a somewhat analogous situation arising in any part of the parks in the western provinces. The difficulty would be that the provinces are charged with responsibility without authority, because the federal parliament under these agreements is the supreme law-making authority.
Let me give another illustration: parliament might, if it so desired, licence the sale of intoxicating liquors in that area while the province might be under prohibition. It might, if it so desired, establish certain institutions wholly at variance with the wish of the province in connection with such matters, and without making regulations subject to the approval of the local authorities, you have created a province within a province, a province-it is called a park-controlled by the federal government, although the privy council has said that under the constitution the province may exercise powers as plenary and ample as the imperial parliament in the fullness of its powers could grant and as this parliament within the ambit of its jurisdiction could exercise. I understand the difficulty of endeavouring to legislate along the lines suggested by the minister, but surely the local authorities should have the right to approve the regulations.

The situation is not likely to be changed, and I submit that when the minister takes the time to look at this more carefully he will find that there is a principle of far-reaching consequences, very, very far-reaching consequences, involved. It means that within a portion of an area of this Dominion called a province, provincial powers shall not be exercised by its legislature, and the federal power which, under the constitution, has no jurisdiction in the premises, is to exercise supreme control over that area and the people settled therein. That is wrong, the same way that it is wrong in respect to a post office in a city, or any part of it. That is a question which, I think, we must settle. The British North America Act provides that there shall be a legislature for each province. I suppose it is customary, as it is in other departments, that a certified cheque or a guarantee accompany any tender so that the government will be protected in the work being carried out satisfactorily to them.

The hon. member has

fMr. Grimmer.]

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY

speechtext:
Mr. GEORGES PARENT (Quebec West) moved the second reading of Bill No. 32, respecting the Interprovincial and James Bay Railway Company.

James Bay Railway

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to know from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) whether this bill would have any prejudicial effect on the Saguenay river and the Chicoutimi district as the nearest point in the province of Quebec to James bay. It appears from the bid that the terminal is proposed to be on the Notta-way river. Would it not be in the interests of the Canadian National Railways not to renew the charter unless the promoters are prepared to build at once? In view of what the country has at stake at Fort Churchill, and that a further outlet on the Saguenay river, where navigation is possible until the end of December, would be of great importance to western Canada, I 'believe nothing should be done that would prevent the Canadian National Railways having that outlet. Therefore I would ask the Minister of Railways to tell the house if anything in this charter might obstruct in the future the development of the plans of the Canadian National Railways in that section?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	The Minister of Railways is
absent at the moment and I can speak only from memory regarding this particular proposal. Two years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway, who own this particular charter, came before parliament and asked for a renewal. The renewal was given then in the same terms as are proposed in this bill, providing for commencement- of construction within two years. This railway runs generally in a northerly direction and is built now as far as Angliers in the province of Quebec, which I believe, is immediately east of lake Timiskamdng, and the proposal is to continue the line from there north-ward to the Nottaway river. 1 am under the impression that my hon. friend from Chicoutimi (Mr. Dubwc) has in mind a line which conceivably might run from the Nottaway eastward to the Saguenay river.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext:
This line would therefore be at right angles to such a proposal and in all probability would not interfere with any possible development from the Nottoway river to Chicoutimi on the Saguenay. In case I should be in error in some of these particulars which I am giving from memory, I presume the bill will be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where it is customary to go very fully into such points as, for instance, that raised by my hon. friend, and to give consideration to any representations for or against the renewal of the charter.
All I can say regarding it at the moment is that it is a very old charter. It will be noticed that it was granted originally in 1901, that a portion of the line has been built, and that the proposal is to give a further two years within which to commence construction of the remainder of the railway. The form of the bill is exactly what the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines has demanded within recent years for such bills, and there is no complaint at all about its form. I think all the matters to which my hon. friend has referred could be very well investigated by that committee when the bill goes there.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very much interested in this question in view of the fact that rather extensive dredging was done in the Saguenay river last summer. Would it not be proper to continue the work so as to have an outlet to James bay from the St. Lawrence through the Saguenay river?

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the promoters of this bill, like a good many other promoters of railways, when they get a charter from this parliament state that they intend to build their railway within a certain time. After the charter is granted they come back to the house for renewal after renewal, and little or nothing is done. It will be noticed that the bill itself does not say that they "shall," or " must," but that they "may." It looks to me very much like a bartering of charters. They get a charter, and possibly because they cannot undertake the work themselves they try to sell it to someone, or get someone interested in it, and if they cannot do that they come back to parliament and ask for a further extension of time. As regards the time specified for completion, it says they "may" commence to construct, and if they do not do it, after a while the conditions may be surrendered and the charter become null and void, but that does not prevent them from asking for a further extension of time under the same conditions. This very bill has been before the house ever since 1901, and we have no guarantee whatever that under this bill anything will be done.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) it is true that this project has been before the house for some years, dating back to 1901. No harm can be done by giving the bill a second reading and referring it to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, in order to give the promoters of the bill an opportunity to

James Bay Railway

be heard, and if they fail to satisfy the committee of their intentions or their bona fides, the committee can very easily turn the proposal down. In the meantime, owing to the vast development which is going on in the northern parts of Quebec and Ontario, especially when we are dealing with such a concern as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I think an opportunity should be afforded to the promoters to be heard. The proposal is a very simple one. They want to develop that part of the country. It is true that they have not been granted as many charters in the west as formerly, because latterly nearly all the railroad construction work in the west has been carried on by the Canadian National Railways at the expense of the whole Dominion of Canada. The promoters of this bill are not asking for this. Ihey are asking merely for an extension of time of two years, to complete in five years. I think it is only fair that the bill should be read a second time and referred to the committee, and if they are not satisfied with the bill they can turn it down.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAY RAIL "WAY COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) has made a point which has been in my mind for some time. The ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) said that this was an old charter. As a matter of fact you and I, Mr. Speaker, were in parliament when this charter was first granted. I was away for eighteen years; I came back, and I find this same old charter. It reminds me of a very important discussion which took place in the old parliament building at least thirty years ago with regard to indiscriminate granting of charters and the perpetual renewal thereof. In spite of the good reasons given for renewal in this case I am sorry to have to differ from mv good friend from Bona venture (Mr. Marcil). I sincerely believe that before this bill >s sent to the committee the history of this company should be given to the house
not that I have any special grudge against this company or this particular project, but because it illustrates the abuses that have taken place in connection with extensions, as pointed out by the hon. member for East Calgary.
It did not take me very long to retrace the history of that slow-going concern. First of all, may I point out that in the bill before us reference is made in the margin to some four statutes. As a matter of fact in the short space of half an hour in the library I picked out ten statutes referring to it. Here is the history of the company: It was incorporated 
in 1901 under the statutes of that year, chapter 66. It was called, as it is now, the Interprovincial and James Bay Railway Company. The provisional directors were gentlemen most of whom I have known, some politicians, some business men, not one of whom, I think, has ever invested one farthing in the venture. The company was to build a line from "a point on the Canadian Pacific railway at or near Lumsden's Mill, to or towards the Des Quinze river." Then various other clauses were incorporated in the charter which was granted before the Railway Act of 1903. I find that in 1903 a subsidy was voted to this company by parliament for fifty miles to be constructed within two years, and an extension of time was granted, the first period having expired, for two further years. That is in chapter 134 of 3 Edward VII. In 1905 the same company came before parliament and received a further extension of time of two years within which to begin the building of the line. In 1906, 6 Edward VII chapter 43, section 42, the subsidy granted in 1903 was renewed. A further extension of time was given to the company to begin the construction of the work that it had undertaken to do in 1901. Six years elapsed and nothing was done. In 1912, the company again came before parliament, and under chapter 106, 2 George V-a change of reign but no change in the system-the company secured from parliament a further extension of time, and it received from parliament at that time a subsidy in lieu of that voted in 1903, again voted n 1906, and never used. Finally, in 1917, sixteen years after the incorporation of the company, a practically new charter was granted; and curiously enough that act, the most important of all the past acts with reference to the company, is not even mentioned in the margin of the bill we have before us.
I wonder how these bills are prepared. The marginal notes are supposed to refer us to all the statutes relating to the company. That I think is important. Some of the statutes mentioned there have no importance whatever. They are either dead letters or repealed; while this act of 1917, which is the material one, which contains the authorization of parliament to this company to contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, is not even mentioned; s,o that we do not know that in dealing with this company we are dealing, to all intents and purposes, with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Is it a matter of prudence on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? How is it that the one material section, which makes reference to the contract to be entered into between this company and the Canadian

James Bay Railway
Pacific Railway Company, which was incorporated in the act of 1917, is not even mentioned?
At all events, in 1917, part of the original charter was repealed; new sections were inserted, and the company was authorized to continue the line. Then came section 8 of that act, which authorized an agreement between the company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for the construction of the same line from Luimsden's Mills to the Des Quinze river. In 1922, five years after this fifth renewal of the charter and five years after the authorization to make the 'bargain with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, this company, serving as a cover for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, again secured the right to continue, if it thought fit, the work which never had been begun. That was twenty-one years after the first charter; it was of age then, but not yet baptized.
In 1924, two years later, there was another definition given with regard to the line to be constructed. The authorization was for the construction of a line from Angliers to the head of the Nottaway river. In the interval, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had built a line which my friend the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) knows was secured by the people of his constituency only after many years of effort.
Then in 1926, under chapter 20, 16-17 George V, the company secured a further extension of time to build that line from Angliers to the head of the Notbaiway river, and in, 1928, under chapter 61, 18-19 George V, the same company secured a further extension of two years, and secured the further right to build a line from Villemairie to some point in the township of Guigues or the township of Nedelec, in the county of Pontiac. I understand neither line has been built.
So, after twenty-nine years, apart from the short line which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company built from Lumsden's Mills to Angliers, no use has been made of the nine charters granted to this company. Is it not time for parliament to reflect upon the privileges it grants to large or small companies to go on year after year, depriving the people of the 'communications to which they are entitled, and very often depriving other enterprises from coming into these fields and accomplishing the same purpose?
The hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dubuc) made reference to some project similar to this, which was designed to connect James bay with the part of the province he represents. In my part of the province there
is a railway line running from Montreal about 160 miles to the northwest. That line was started by a small colonization company; they did some work, although they were under great handicaps, and finally they sold their charter and their rights to the Canadian Pacific railway. I represented the same constituency some thirty years ago, when we secured the construction of that line to the point where it now ends. For twenty years now there have been demands not only from the people of the constituency, but from the chambers of commerce and the trading people of Montreal to have this line serve as a connecting link between the city of Montreal and the transcontinental line, which was built with money collected through taxes from all the people of Canada. I believe the one million people living in Montreal paid their share of the amount of money invested in the transcontinental line, and therefore they are entitled bo have some connection with it. Now .they have to go down to Quebec or connect with the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway in order to link up with the transcontinental line.
I repeat, is it not time for us to look over these charters and see that the companies either make use of them or abandon their rights? Is it not the duty of this parliament to see that our statutes do not remain filled with unused charters which block other enterprising people who might be disposed to construct different lines of rail? The whole country is interested in seeing that privileges granted by parliament are not abused by either large or small companies.
Privileges of this kind may be abused in two ways. Abuse may take the form of squandering the money of the people in venturesome enterprises which are not justified; or abuse may consist of not making use of the powers granted by parliament, whether by this company, by the Algoma Central Company, by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or by any other concern. When they receive charters granted under our Railway Act, they are given practically sovereign powers. They are given the power of expropriation; they are permitted to pass through public and private property. Surely parliament does not give these powers just for the sake of giving them. Parliament does not invest these companies with such enormous privileges merely to enable them to make or to lose money. We are supposed to grant charters in the public interest ; we are supposed to invest companies with the power of constructing railways for the benefit of the trading public and for the benefit of settlers. Lines are often built to open up a country and to enable people who are in
James Bay Railway

quest of virgin land to settle on farms and have communication with the centres of population. If the privileges distributed for these reasons remain unused by those who receive them, it works to the detriment of the public as a whole, and parliament is remiss in its duty if that situation is not remedied. This point has been in my mind for many years. It was discussed in the old parliament. I remember very well the excellent declarations and speches made by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, by the late Mr. Blair, by the late Sir Charles Tupper and by Sir George Foster. The Railway Act of 1903 was largely the outcome of those discussions. That act was the consolidation of the various acts which had been passed previously as well as a standardization of the charters to which the acting minister has referred. It was not only to change the law that we made that reform, it was not only to see that every company, large or small, would receive a charter with the same number of standard clauses in it: it was mainly for the purpose of preventing an abuse which deprived the trading public at large of the benefit of railway construction. It would seem as though we are to have several similar bills before us and it is time that we had a declaration from the government as to whether or not they intend to implement engagements entered into twentydive years ago. After eighteen years' absence from this house I begin to ask myself if I am not a Rip Van Winkle, because when I return I find the abuses which were to be corrected by the com-binded wisdom and genius of all parties still existing.
There is the further point brought up by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dubuc). The actual results of the navigation of Hudson bay are not known. It is not known whether there will be sufficient trade to support four or five lines running to James bay or Hudson bay. The Hudson bay venture was ratified by parliament largely for the benefit of the western provinces; but I aim quite sure that our western friends would be the first to say that the people of the eastern provinces, especially of Ontario and Quebec, are entitled to their fair share of the return trade from Europe which may cotme over that route. It seems to me that we should not keep on granting charters for railway lines to connect with that sheet of water or as some say that sheet of ice, when we do not know how many lines will be needed. The amount of trade which will accrue is unknown, and if we continue to renew charters to different companies to build lines from James bay westward, from James bay southward, or from James bay eastward, without knowing what

the results will be, it will be some time before any one line is built. Any one company might- hesitate in expending capital when they know that other rival lines may be built.
I do not say that we should hold these companies strictly to the two year limit; but there should be some limit, as the railway companies seem to consider that these renewals are a permanent privilege and that this parliament will renew a charter every time it is asked. In the light of these past exiperiences, I think the house should hesitate before committing itself to the principle of the renewal of charters without a good reason being given why such renewal should be -made.
Motion agreed to on division and bill read the second time.

maintopic: ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY

speechtext: Mr. J. A. BRADETTE (North Timiskam-ing) moved the second reading of Bill No. 33, respecting the Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company.

maintopic: ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, the explanation in the margin of this bill reads:
Extension of time for construction and completion of certain line of railway.
This explanation should read as follows: Extension of time for construction and completion of a certain portion of a certain line of railway.
This railway has constructed nearly 300 miles of line, 200 miles of which is main line and 80 miles being extensions. Two years ago this company -came before parliament and asked for an extension of their charter, which was granted, but they have not been able to carry on the construction work proposed, a-nd I hope the house will grant the further extension which is now asked for.
The first -charter was granted to this corporation in 1890, for the building of a main line from hault Ste. Marie to Fran-z on the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway. A few years afterward another charter was granted for the extension of the line from Franz to Hearst, and, -as I said 'before. this company has under operation nearly 300 -miles of main line running from Sault Ste. Marie -to Hearst, and nearly 100 -miles of branch lines. A few years ago they operated a weekly passenger service; this was later changed to a tri-weekly service, but last year they inaugurated a daily passenger service from Sault Ste. Marie to Hearst. When the first charter was given the provincial government granted

Hudson Bay Railway
1,500.000 acres of land, and 500.000 acres went with the second charter. Most of that land is mineral and timber land, a great deal of which has been 'parcelled out and is under development. Practically from Franz to Hearst most of that section has been open to colonization. We have some very progressive colonization settlements in places like Sbavert, Coppell, and so forth, which are well known through our section of the country.
I believe no objection will be put forward in regard to the other extension going northward, because those who belonged to the railway committee in the first session of the new parliament, 1927, are fully aware of my activities in two instances with respect to applications for the granting of charters to two newly formed railway companies. An application of a private corporation for a charter for the construction of a railway into the Red lake district was defeated largely by my activities. The same also applies to an application in connection with a proposed privately constructed railway from Iroquois falls to the southern part of James bay, which I claim was also defeated on account of my objections.
Some hon. gentlemen may think this railway will run parallel to the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. It is true it will be running parallel northward, but the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario is 135 miles eastward of the eventual construction of the extension. Every hon. member, at least from Ontario, is fully aware of the activities of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario commission and its alertness in railway matters and so far I have not heard any objection to the extension of that charter to the Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company. This company has been capitalized in the sum of nearly 85,000,000. Most of that money has been spent and so far no dividends have been paid to the shareholders. They have their main line in first class condition. They have been working on the road-bed for the last five or six years in a very effective manner and that line compares favourably with any publicly-owned railway or the Canadian Pacific. Therefore I believe this bill will receive the sanction of the house.
Speaking of the eventual extension from Hearst northwards which will tap the Albany river, I repeat that this extension will not enter info conflict with the present extension of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway from Cochrane to James bay, which very likely will have a terminal for years to come at Moose Factory, because it is nearly 100 miles from Albany to Moose Factory. Marie, that is the Soo line, with a station called Franz on the Canadian Pacific main line, and the other from Franz on the Canadian Pacific to Hearst on the Canadian National. This request to renew the powers of the company to tap the Hudson bay basin has been renewed, I do not know how many times; but what has been built is but a fraction of what was supposed to be built and what this company has been asking for and has been keeping in reserve on paper for years without making use of it. Hudson Bay Railway

think, still holds a charter to connect the Hudson bay somewhere with the Joliette branch of the Canadian Pacific; the one mentioned by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dubuc), and, I think, another one which is supposed to come down the St. Maurice valley, we have at the present time charters enabling various companies to build an open fan of railways all starting from James bay to come and tap-what? I think it is another one of those charters which the great company holds in its hand to prevent any competition from coming within its territory, or even to prevent the national railway of Canada, to the success of which we are supposed to be devoted, from competing; because this is in the way of any railway that might be built from any point on the Canadian National railway to tap Hudson bay.

I do not know enough about that. It is so complicated, as between Quebec and Ontario, and various companies, that I do not know about it; but I do know about these charters. We have had the same difficulty. It took us twenty years to secure the construction of the line that had been started from Montreal to St. Jerome and then from St. Jerome to Ste. Agathe. I am sorry the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Prevost) is not present. I saw the beginning of the line from St. Jerome to Ste. Agathe. It remained! there for about twenty years and then was brought up to a certain point on the Red river, then called Chute aux Iroquois, which is now called Labelle. Later we secured the construction of thirty miles further. So it took about thirty years to connect one of the best centres of colonization of the province 
of Quebec with the city of Montreal, 160 miles distant. Do our western friends realize that? They very rightly complain, time and again, of the difficulty they have had in getting railway communication; but do they know that in the oldest province of Canada there are regions capable of settlement and culture, within 150 miles of Montreal, which have yet no communication, because practically the whole of the railway system of Quebec is in the hands of either the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National? The Canadian National Railways are entirely bound to their old trunk lines and the Canadian Pacific is in pretty much the same position. As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, the Canadian Pacific has certainly helped colonization; but as the late Lord Shaughnessy said to me once, when I went to see him to have this colonization road constructed through my constituency, "My dear sir, you must realize that this is a business enterprise. We cannot build a line just for the sake of giving transportation facilities to help people. We are out to get traffic, andi we are not going to spend money to provide transportation facilities for people who will not furnish the traffic to justify the expenditure." I made this observation to Lord Shaughnessy:	"Do
you not realize that by building branch lines you are opening up new territory, bringing in new settlers, creating more traffic for your road? The settlers that your branch line will bring in will build butter and cheese factories, they will cut the hardwood which is now rotting in the woods because it is impossible to transport it by water." That caught his imagination; he built that branch line; and to-day it is one of the best paying branch lines of the Canadian Pacific. For each of twenty years there was only a small tourist traffic for about three months and the rest of the year the traffic was not sufficient to pay for the coal and grease necessary to run the trains. To-day, as I said, it is one of the best paying branch lines of the Canadian Pacific. It has opened up new territory. It has brought people in there who would otherwise now be working in the factories of New England, and would be lost to the province of Quebec and to Canada, to agriculture and industry in this country. By building that branch line the Canadian Pacific have increased their traffic; they have contributed to increasing the population and developing the agriculture and trade of that portion of the province.
The same is true of any other branch line constructed as a colonization enterprise. In the west the farmers, of course, have to cope with the very long distances, because coloni-

Highwood Western Railway
zation has been scattered over an immense area. In our province the people have another kind of difficulty to contend with, and that is the hard and costly work of the forest settler, who has to spend time and money for three or four or five years, or employ the labour of his own family, in clearing the land, and during those years all he receives by way of return is the proceeds from the sale of a few logs. Colonization in northern Quebec and northern Ontario is extremely hard, but we have in those northern regions a remnant of what was formerly the hardiest and most courageous breed of settlers known to the world.

No; they were the

Some of them would go and cut wood there for one or two years, but they needed communications. Roads were extremely difficult to build through the bush. It is true that the governments of both Ontario and Quebec have done a great deal to help the settlement of these northern territories; but the farther you get from the large centres the greater is the need of railway communication. Besides you cannot expect the settler in the forest to-day to be so utterly different from other human beings of his own age that he will work as his forefathers did fifty years ago. He demands more facilities, and his children ask for more advantages. They will not stay in the bush to be eaten up by the black-

No, by the black flies. To-day they will not stay three or four or five or six years up in that northern territory with practically no communication with the civilized world. They ask for better roads. They wish to have a small Ford car as soon as possible, and they ask for railway communication to ship their hard-won produce to the large centres. These people deserve consideration. We in the province of Quebec are in full sympathy with the settlers of the western provinces and with their endeavour to get better railway facilities, but surely we in the province of Quebec are entitled to some sympathy from them in our effort to help our own people, who have done their share, and are still doing their share, in building up Canada. which our people have to face, and to speak of the abuses that there have been in the granting of railway charters to companies that keep them in their portfolio, and sometimes issue bonds, although I do not think they can do that now, but at all events prevent other companies from constructing a road through that territory, thereby depriving the country of the advantages that would be derived from sensible legislation which I 'hope this parliament in its wisdom will pass before very long.

How much is this going to cost altogether?
The total estimated cost is $30,000.
Ten thousand dollars for the wharf?
Ten thousand dollars for the wharf, $18,460 for the cribwork, $1,000 for levelling surface, and $540 estimated for contingencies.

In giving the details the minister stated that this was a very dilapidated wharf and that practically the only thing left of value was the filling. The minister estimated the filling as being valued at 60 cents per cubic yard, or a total of $7,200. What is the additional amount being paid for?
That is for the rest of the wharf.
You say it is dilapidated and of no value.
The purchase of the site and everything else, except the filling.

Item agreed to.
Bonaventure-rebuilding protection works,

Would the minister give us the details of this item?

Questions
This is to construct a breakwater which was commenced during 1928-29.
Why is the amount $1,200 instead of $2,800 or $3,600, or some other figure.

The amount is required to complete the construction of a breakwater 100 feet in length by 18 feet in width in round timber open faced cribwork, well ballasted with stone and sheathed and covered with spruce deals. The estimated cost is given at $1,700; materials purchased in 1928-29, $500; and balance required to complete $1,200.
That is all the information the minister has?
That is all that appears in the engineer's report.
There was no work done last summer.
Just materials purchased.

Item agreed to.
Bradore Bay-wharf, $47,000.
What constituency is that in?

It is in the constituency
of Oharlevoiix-Saguenay. There is a revote of $5,000 from 1929-30, and this work is under contract.
What is the total contract price?
It is given as $60,334.

I am not familiar with
the geography of this district, and I would appreciate the minister's advising me if there ia anything in the estimates for Anticosti island.
No.

It is Beauharnois this
year.

Item agreed to.
Cap de la Madeleine-in full and final settlement of the claim of Messrs. Munm & Shea in connection with their contract for w'harf extension, $27,249.25.
We should have some explanation of this item. This would appear to be one of those cases where the contractor had taken the contract at too low a price and there are extras now to be paid.

The water conditions at
this point were very unusual, and upon examination it was found that it cost S54,00C more than the contract price to construct, and the recommendation was made that we make up the difference. After very careful consideration it was decided that the company should pay half and that we should bear half the loss.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this item carry?

No, it should be held
over.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
